items.stem: In September 1955 Mamie Till-Mobley made one decision that put her son's murder in Mississippi before a national audience and into the early history of the Civil Rights Movement. What was it?
items.stemEs: En septiembre de 1955, Mamie Till-Mobley tomó una decisión que puso el asesinato de su hijo en Misisipi ante un público nacional y en la historia temprana del Movimiento por los Derechos Civiles. ¿Cuál fue?

choices.text: She travelled to Sumner, Mississippi and testified at the trial, identifying her son's body for the court
choices.textEs: Viajó a Sumner, Misisipi, y testificó en el juicio, identificando el cuerpo de su hijo ante el tribunal
choices.explanation: She did testify, in September 1955, and did so under conditions that took considerable courage. Testimony in a Mississippi courtroom reached the jury that acquitted the killers; the decision in the question reached everyone else.
choices.misconception: answers with the courageous act inside the trial rather than the one outside it

choices.text: She joined speaking tours organised by the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, which carried the case to Northern audiences
choices.textEs: Se unió a giras de conferencias organizadas por la Asociación Nacional para el Progreso de las Personas de Color, que llevaron el caso a públicos del norte
choices.explanation: She did speak at such events, including large rallies that autumn, and they mattered. They followed the decision in the question and drew their audiences from it; a speaking tour reaches a hall, and the photograph reached the country.
choices.misconception: takes a consequence of the decision for the decision itself

choices.text: She insisted on an open casket, so that the condition of the body could be seen and photographed
choices.textEs: Insistió en un ataúd abierto, para que el estado del cuerpo pudiera verse y fotografiarse

choices.text: She had the funeral held in Mississippi, so that local people would be made to confront what had happened in their own county
choices.textEs: Hizo que el funeral se celebrara en Misisipi, para que la gente del lugar tuviera que enfrentarse a lo ocurrido en su propio condado
choices.explanation: The direction was the opposite. Mississippi authorities wanted a quick local burial and she fought to have the body sent north to Chicago, where her son had lived and where the national Black press could photograph it.
choices.misconception: reverses the direction she moved her son's body and the audience she was seeking

items.dokRationale: Recall of one decision and what it accomplished. The student retrieves an action; no reasoning about how the coverage interacted with the verdict is involved. A DOK 2 item on this standard requires that reasoning.
items.explanation: She refused the quiet burial Mississippi officials wanted and had the body brought to Chicago with the casket left open, saying she wanted the world to see what had been done. Tens of thousands came to the church, and the photographs ran in Jet and the Chicago Defender — which is how a county killing became a national fact.
items.explanationEs: Rechazó el entierro discreto que querían las autoridades de Misisipi e hizo trasladar el cuerpo a Chicago con el ataúd abierto, diciendo que quería que el mundo viera lo que se había hecho. Decenas de miles acudieron a la iglesia, y las fotografías aparecieron en Jet y en el Chicago Defender: así un crimen de condado se convirtió en un hecho nacional.

items.stem: Jet magazine published the photograph of Emmett Till's body in September 1955, and an all-white jury in Sumner, Mississippi acquitted the two men charged with his murder later the same month. What does that pairing show about the role of mass media in the Civil Rights Movement?
items.stemEs: La revista Jet publicó la fotografía del cuerpo de Emmett Till en septiembre de 1955, y un jurado compuesto solo por blancos en Sumner, Misisipi, absolvió ese mismo mes a los dos hombres acusados de su asesinato. ¿Qué muestra esa combinación sobre el papel de los medios de comunicación masiva en el Movimiento por los Derechos Civiles?

choices.text: Southern newspapers did not report the trial, so only the Northern press carried the story to the public
choices.textEs: Los periódicos del sur no informaron del juicio, de modo que solo la prensa del norte llevó la historia al público
choices.explanation: Southern papers covered the trial heavily — dozens of reporters filled the Sumner courtroom and the Jackson and Memphis dailies ran it at length. What differed was the framing and whether the photograph of the body was printed, not whether the story was told.
choices.misconception: mistakes a difference in how a story was told for the absence of any coverage

choices.text: Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery three months later, and said afterward that she had been thinking of Emmett Till when she did it
choices.textEs: Rosa Parks se negó a ceder su asiento en un autobús en Montgomery tres meses después, y dijo luego que estaba pensando en Emmett Till cuando lo hizo
choices.explanation: True, and it is the clearest single piece of evidence that the coverage carried. It is an effect of what the media did rather than a statement about what the media could do, which is what the pairing in the question is about.
choices.misconception: offers the strongest consequence in place of the mechanism that produced it

choices.text: The two men sold a confession to Look magazine in 1956 and could not be tried for the murder a second time
choices.textEs: Los dos hombres vendieron una confesión a la revista Look en 1956 y no pudieron ser juzgados por el asesinato una segunda vez
choices.explanation: Entirely true, and it is the sharpest illustration of how final the acquittal was: having been tried once they were protected from a second trial, and they were paid to describe the killing. It answers what happened next, not what the pairing shows.
choices.misconception: reports the episode's most striking sequel instead of reading the two facts together

choices.text: A national audience could be reached even where the local verdict went the other way, so the case mattered beyond the court that decided it
choices.textEs: Se podía llegar a un público nacional incluso donde el veredicto local iba en sentido contrario, de modo que el caso importó más allá del tribunal que lo decidió

items.dokRationale: The student must read two outcomes against each other — a national audience and a local acquittal — and say what the first could do that the second could not undo. Recalling either fact on its own is the DOK 1 version of this content.
items.explanation: A jury verdict is final and local; a photograph is neither. The acquittal closed the only forum that could have punished the killers, and the coverage opened one the county had no authority over, which is why the case kept working after the law had finished with it. Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery three months later and said afterward that she had thought of Till.
items.explanationEs: Un veredicto de jurado es definitivo y local; una fotografía no es ninguna de las dos cosas. La absolución cerró el único foro que habría podido castigar a los asesinos, y la cobertura abrió uno sobre el que el condado no tenía autoridad alguna; por eso el caso siguió actuando después de que la ley hubiera terminado con él. Rosa Parks fue detenida en Montgomery tres meses después y dijo luego que había pensado en Till.

items.stem: Historians place Emmett Till's murder at a turning point in the trajectory of the Civil Rights Movement even though no one was ever punished for it. What best explains that judgement?
items.stemEs: Los historiadores sitúan el asesinato de Emmett Till en un punto de inflexión de la trayectoria del Movimiento por los Derechos Civiles aunque nadie fue castigado nunca por él. ¿Qué explica mejor ese juicio?

choices.text: It persuaded the Supreme Court to decide Brown v. Board of Education against segregated schooling
choices.textEs: Persuadió a la Corte Suprema de decidir Brown contra la Junta de Educación en contra de la escolarización segregada
choices.explanation: Brown is real and it is the other great landmark of these years — decided in May 1954, more than a year BEFORE the murder. The sequence runs the other way: the decision was part of the climate in which Mississippi reacted as it did.
choices.misconception: reverses the order of two landmarks fifteen months apart

choices.text: It gave the movement a national audience and a shared sense of urgency that the acquittal could not take away
choices.textEs: Dio al movimiento un público nacional y un sentido compartido de urgencia que la absolución no podía quitarle

choices.text: It produced the first federal anti-lynching statute, which Congress passed in 1957 over Southern opposition
choices.textEs: Produjo la primera ley federal contra los linchamientos, que el Congreso aprobó en 1957 pese a la oposición del sur
choices.explanation: Congress did pass a civil rights act in 1957, the first since Reconstruction, and Southern senators fought it hard. It created the Civil Rights Division and a commission and dealt with voting; it was not an anti-lynching law. A federal anti-lynching statute carrying Till's name was not enacted until 2022.
choices.misconception: merges the 1957 civil rights act with the anti-lynching law that took another sixty-five years

choices.text: It ended the practice of seating all-white juries in Mississippi murder trials, which no court had limited before then
choices.textEs: Puso fin a la práctica de integrar jurados exclusivamente blancos en los juicios por asesinato en Misisipi, que ningún tribunal había limitado hasta entonces
choices.explanation: That practice continued for decades. Black Mississippians were largely barred from the voter rolls the jury lists were drawn from, and the Supreme Court did not limit the striking of jurors by race until Batson v. Kentucky in 1986.
choices.misconception: places a reform that took three more decades at the moment of the injustice that prompted it

items.dokRationale: The student has to separate a case's legal outcome from its historical effect and explain why the second can be large when the first is nothing. Three options name real events of the period that the case did not in fact produce.
items.explanation: A turning point is measured in what it made possible, not in what it settled. The case cost nothing legally and supplied the movement with something organising could use: a national audience that had seen the photograph, a fourteen-year-old whose death no one could explain away, and the knowledge that a Mississippi courtroom would not supply justice on its own.
items.explanationEs: Un punto de inflexión se mide por lo que hizo posible, no por lo que resolvió. El caso no costó nada en lo legal y dio al movimiento algo que la organización podía usar: un público nacional que había visto la fotografía, un muchacho de catorce años cuya muerte nadie podía justificar, y la certeza de que un tribunal de Misisipi no daría justicia por sí solo.
